nations: Southern Ute;Ute Mountain Ute;Ute Indian Tribe of Utah;Kiowa;Comanche;Apache of Oklahoma;Eastern Shoshone;Northern Cheyenne;Northern Arapaho;Cheyenne and Arapaho of Oklahoma
instrument: Indian Trade and Intercourse Act of 1834, Art. 1 (as cited for congressional title)
summary: TREC selected nations using three legal criteria: aboriginal (original/Indian) title from initial and continuous use; congressional (reserved) title, where Congress legislated the land as Indian Country, citing the 1834 Trade and Intercourse Act Art. 1; and treaty title, for tribes that signed treaties with the US about land now in Colorado.
verbatim_quote: Congressional title, or reserved title, indicates that Congress has enacted legislation acknowledging the title of the land as Indian Country, as seen in the Indian Trade and non-Intercourse Act of 1834, Article 1.
federal_account_contrast: Royce/Kappler record only treaty cessions. TREC adds aboriginal and congressional title as separate layers of legal interest that existed before and alongside any cession.
map_implication: Model three title layers per nation (aboriginal, congressional/Indian Country under 1834 Act, treaty) rather than a single ceded/not ceded polygon state.
notes: This is TREC's framework, not a disputed fact. The 1834 Act is the Act of June 30, 1834, 4 Stat. 729 (cite added by reader, not in source).

summary: TREC itself used the Royce maps to identify nations involved in cessions, and reproduces a 'Royce Map showing ceded Indian Lands in Colorado 1896'. It states that historical documents, especially treaties, carry pervasive bias and that firsthand American Indian accounts are scarce.
verbatim_quote: The scarcity of firsthand American Indian accounts further exacerbates this bias
federal_account_contrast: TREC uses the same Royce base the atlas uses, but reads it as evidence of who was dispossessed and under what circumstances, not as proof of lawful transfer.
map_implication: Label Royce layer as 'recorded cessions (federal record)' and add a caveat that the record carries bias and omits Native accounts.
notes: Useful for framing: even a Native-led commission depends on Royce, so the problem is presentation, not the base data.

instrument: Indian Claims Commission claims of the ten nations
summary: TREC reviewed ICC reports for every nation. It states land was central in every claim but not one acre was returned, and argues this departs from other land disputes where possession was typically restored.
verbatim_quote: Despite land being a central issue in every claim, not a single acre was returned to the possession of Tribal Nations.
sources_cited_by_source: ICC reports (dockets not named in this chunk)
federal_account_contrast: The federal framing treats ICC awards as settling title. TREC frames them as money paid in place of land, a discriminatory remedy.
map_implication: Where an ICC docket 'extinguished' title by payment, mark the polygon as 'title extinguished by ICC payment; no land returned' rather than 'ceded by treaty'. Pull docket numbers from the tribal chapters.
notes: The claim that possession is 'typically restored' in non-Indian land disputes is a general legal assertion without citation here.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes (intro + exec summary)
summary: Executive summary says critics argue the ICC was unfair, returned no land, and paid no compounding interest on awards. TREC recommends Congress correct the ICC's construction, discriminatory processes and implementation.
verbatim_quote: Critics argue that the ICC lacked fairness in its process and failed to return any land to the Indian Nations. The lack of compounding interest on awards also raises legal questions.
federal_account_contrast: Federal account presents ICC as final settlement. TREC flags no land return and no interest as structural defects.
map_implication: For ICC-adjudicated areas, show award amount and valuation date with a note that awards carried no interest and no land.
notes: Recommendation p25: 'correct the vast issues involved in the construction, discriminatory processes, and implementation of the Indian Claims Commission.' Act is 60 Stat. 1049 (reader addition).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes (intro + exec summary)
nations: Tribal Nations holding congressional title in Colorado
instrument: Indian Trade and Intercourse Act of 1834
summary: The 1834 Act defined Indian country as land where Indian title was not extinguished, barred land transactions without a treaty, and penalized settlement or survey on Indian lands. TREC says it was violated many times with compensation rarely if ever paid, and recommends Congress compensate nations with congressional title for the unauthorized invasion.
verbatim_quote: It prohibited land transactions without a treaty, with penalties for settlements or surveys on Indian lands. ... This act was violated numerous times and compensation was rarely if ever paid.
federal_account_contrast: Settlement before cession (e.g. 1858-61 gold rush settlement) was illegal under federal law itself; Royce dates only the later cession.
map_implication: For areas settled before their cession date, show the settlement as illegal under the 1834 Act and show the gap between occupation and legal cession.
notes: 4 Stat. 729 (reader addition).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes (intro + exec summary)
summary: TREC says land transferred under the 1861 Fort Wise Treaty lacked required signatures; attempts to fix this at the time failed, so the transfers were illegal. It recommends Congress and Colorado resolve the illegal transfer under Article 6 by restoring land taken from the Northern Cheyenne or Northern Arapaho.
verbatim_quote: Despite attempts to rectify the error at the time, the necessary signatures were not obtained resulting in illegal transfers.
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows the Fort Wise area as ceded by treaty. TREC says the Northern bands' signatures, required under the treaty, were never obtained.
map_implication: Flag the Fort Wise cession polygon as 'cession incomplete: required Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho signatures never obtained (TREC)'. Show it as contested, not ceded.
notes: Fort Wise Treaty Feb 18, 1861, 12 Stat. 1163 (reader addition). Royce area not stated in source; reader believes it is Royce 477, verify. Article 6 content to be confirmed in Arapaho/Cheyenne chapters.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes (intro + exec summary)
place: Colorado State University land grant parcels
summary: CSU received Morrill Act grants funded by illegal or coerced dispossession, still owns much of its original parcels (managed by the State Land Board) and earns revenue from mineral and grazing leases. TREC recommends CSU return the remaining 19,000 acres, an independent commission to manage the assets, free room, board and tuition for Native students, and a vet program cohort of at least 10 Native students a year.
verbatim_quote: We recommend that CSU return the remaining 19,000 acres of land of the original land grant to those Tribal Nations that it was illegally taken from.
federal_account_contrast: Morrill grants appear as federal land gifts; TREC traces them to dispossession and continuing revenue.
map_implication: Add CSU Morrill parcels (about 19,000 acres retained) as a layer linked to the cessions they came from.
notes: Congress-level rec p24: all Morrill land-grant institutions give free tuition and room and board to descendants of affected nations. 12 Stat. 503 (reader addition).

nations: Tribal Nations that ceded land in Colorado
summary: TREC says treaties did not address water rights, so unless Congress expressly excluded them, nations retain them as inherent reserved rights. Recommends Congress and Interior calculate water rights taken without permission.
verbatim_quote: Water rights were not explicitly addressed in the treaties, meaning that unless Congress specifically stated that they were not included, it is within the inherent powers of Indian Nations to have reserved them without notice.
federal_account_contrast: Cession framing implies water went with land; TREC argues it was reserved.
map_implication: Add a 'water rights not addressed in instrument' attribute to cessions.
notes: Legal theory, close to the reserved-rights doctrine (Winters v. US, 1908) but extended to ceded lands, which is not settled law. Source cites no case.

summary: TREC asserts subsurface minerals not addressed in treaties belong to American Indians unless proven otherwise, and that uncompensated extraction harmed the Ute economy. Recommends Congress compensate for minerals on ceded lands not specifically released.
verbatim_quote: If certain subsurface minerals were not addressed in any treaties or explicitly mentioned, they are considered to belong to American Indians unless proven otherwise.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats cession as full title transfer.
map_implication: Attribute: 'mineral rights not expressly ceded (TREC claim)' on Ute cessions, pending check of instrument text.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes (intro + exec summary)
instrument: State trust lands; Colorado State Board of Land Commissioners
summary: The State Land Board, Colorado's second largest landowner, manages a $4.1 billion endowment for K-12 schools with no public accounting of holdings from Native cessions. Trust lands earn revenue from grazing, logging, mining and oil and gas; tribes have no control. TREC recommends a full public audit of the Public School Fund and Land Board, and that the School Fund and Land Board identify illegally taken land and fund extra support for Native students.
verbatim_quote: There has never been a public accounting of land holdings that originated from Native legal or illegal land cessions.
federal_account_contrast: Shows dispossession as ongoing revenue ('theft in perpetuity'), not a closed historical event.
map_implication: Add Colorado state trust land parcels as a layer intersected with Royce areas.
notes: Section heading 'THEFT IN PERPETUITY' (p21).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes (intro + exec summary)
instrument: Peace Commission 1867-68; rider to the Indian Appropriations Act
summary: TREC says Congress eliminated Native sovereign rights without input or legal justification, and that the military-led Peace Commission of 1867-68 aimed to remove all nations under a peace pretext. Recommends Congress rescind the Appropriations Act rider and re-establish the right of Native Nations to negotiate treaties.
verbatim_quote: We recommend that the US Congress rescind the rider to the Indian Appropriations Act that denies Tribal sovereignty and re-establish the right of Native Nations to negotiate treaties.
federal_account_contrast: Peace Commission treaties (e.g. Medicine Lodge 1867, Fort Laramie 1868) are recorded as peace treaties; TREC frames them as removal instruments.
map_implication: Tag 1867-68 Peace Commission treaties with 'removal purpose (TREC)'.
notes: Rider year not stated; it is the Act of March 3, 1871, 16 Stat. 566 (reader addition).

place: Colorado boarding and industrial schools; 180 school districts
summary: TREC commissioned studies of HB 1192 implementation across 180 districts, K-12 Indian education including 1800s boarding and industrial schools, and higher education.
